q: Identify the function of lipase in the process of digestion.
solution:
The correct answer is Breaking down emulsified fats. Key Points

• Lipase is an enzyme that plays a crucial role in the digestion of fats in the body.

• The breakdown of fats is essential for the absorption and utilization of essential fatty acids and fat-soluble vitamins.

• Lipase breaks down emulsified fats:

• The process of digestion starts in the mouth where the food is chewed and mixed with saliva.

• Saliva contains an enzyme called salivary lipase that starts breaking down fats.

• However, the majority of fat digestion happens in the small intestine where the emulsified fats are acted upon by pancreatic lipase.

• This enzyme breaks down the emulsified fats into fatty acids and glycerol, which can be absorbed by the body.

• Lipase works with bile:

• Bile is a digestive fluid produced by the liver and stored in the gallbladder.

• Bile contains bile salts that help in the emulsification of fats, making them easier for lipase to break down.

• Lipase and bile work together to digest fats and ensure their absorption in the body.

• Lipase deficiency can lead to malabsorption:

• In some cases, people may have a deficiency of lipase, which can result in malabsorption of fats.

• This can lead to symptoms like bloating, gas, diarrhea, and weight loss.

• People with conditions like cystic fibrosis, pancreatitis, and celiac disease may have a deficiency of lipase.

Additional Information

• Breaking down roughage: This is the function of enzymes like cellulase, which break down the fiber in plant foods.

• Lipase does not play a role in breaking down roughage.

• Secreting intestinal fluids: This is the function of the intestinal glands, which secrete fluids that help in the digestion and absorption of nutrients.

• Lipase is not involved in this process.

• Digesting proteins: This is the function of enzymes like pepsin and trypsin, which break down proteins into amino acids.

• Lipase does not play a role in digesting proteins.

• Hence, the correct option is 2) Breaking down emulsified fats.

Additional Information

• Algae are a diverse group of aquatic organisms that can range from single-celled organisms to large seaweeds.

• Pteridophytes are vascular plants that reproduce by spores instead of seeds.

• They have true roots, stems, and leaves, and can range from small herbaceous plants to large tree ferns.

• The alternation of generations is a life cycle that includes both a haploid (n) gametophyte and a diploid (2n) sporophyte stage.

q: Which condition, also known as icterus, causes a yellowing of your skin and the whites of your eyes?
solution:

• Jaundice (Icterus) is a condition where the skin, the whites of the eyes (sclera), and sometimes other tissues develop a yellow tint.

• This yellowing happens because of an excessive buildup of a substance called bilirubin in the blood.

• Bilirubin is a yellow pigment produced during the normal breakdown of red blood cells.

• Normally, the liver processes bilirubin and excretes it into bile, which helps digest fats.

• The bile is then eliminated from the body through stool.

• Pre-hepatic (before the liver):

• Caused by increased destruction of red blood cells (hemolysis).

• Examples: Sickle cell anaemia, malaria.

• Hepatic (in the liver):

• Caused by liver diseases that impair its ability to process bilirubin.

• Examples: Hepatitis, cirrhosis, alcoholic liver disease.

• Post-hepatic (after the liver):

• Caused by an obstruction in bile ducts that prevents bilirubin from being excreted.

• Examples: Gallstones, tumors, bile duct strictures.

Additional Information

• This system is different from mammals and birds, which have a double circulatory system.

• Blood flows through the gill filaments where gas exchange occurs – carbon dioxide is released into the water and oxygen is absorbed.

• Adaptations

• The two-chambered heart and single circulatory system are highly adapted to an aquatic environment where oxygen levels can vary.

• These adaptations ensure efficient oxygen delivery to support the metabolism and activity levels of fishes.

• Platyhelminthes includes flatworms like Tapeworms.

Additional Information

• Annelida:

• Annelida, also known as segmented worms, are characterized by their segmented body structure.

• Examples include Earthworms, Leeches, and Polychaetes.

• They have a true coelom and a well-developed nervous system.

• Arthropoda:

• Arthropoda is the largest phylum in the animal kingdom, including insects, arachnids, myriapods, and crustaceans.

• They have an exoskeleton, segmented bodies, and jointed appendages.

• Examples include Ants, Spiders, Crabs, and Centipedes.

• Echinodermata:

• Echinodermata are marine animals characterized by their radial symmetry and a water vascular system.

• Examples include Sea stars, Sea urchins, and Sea cucumbers.

• They have a calcareous endoskeleton composed of ossicles.

• Platyhelminthes:

• Platyhelminthes, also known as flatworms, are characterized by their flattened body structure.

• They are acoelomates (lack a true body cavity) and have a simple digestive system with only one opening.

• Examples include Tapeworms, Flukes, and Planarians.

q: Microbes like Rhizobium, Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter are used for:
solution:
The correct answer is nitrogen cycling.

Key Points

•
Nitrogen Cycle-

• Nitrogen is an essential constituent of protein and is a basic building block of all living tissue. It constitutes nearly 16% by weight of all the proteins that is, converted to ammonia, nitrites or nitrates before it can be taken up by plants.

• Nitrogen fixation on earth is accomplished in three different ways:

a) By microorganisms (bacteria and blue-green algae)

b) By man using industrial processes (fertilizer factories) and

c) To a limited extent by atmospheric phenomena such as thunder and lighting

• Certain microorganisms are capable of fixing atmospheric nitrogen into ammonium ions. These include free-living nitrifying bacteria (e.g. aerobic Azotobacter and anaerobic Clostridium) and symbiotic nitrifying bacteria living in association with leguminous plants and symbiotic bacteria living in non-leguminous root nodule plants (e.g. Rhizobium) as well as blue-green algae (e.g. Anabaena, Spirulina).

• Ammonium ions can be directly taken up as a source of nitrogen by some plants, or are oxidized to nitrites or nitrates by two groups of specialised bacteria: Nitrosomonas bacteria promote the transformation of ammonia into nitrite. Nitrite is then further transformed into nitrate by the bacteria Nitrobacter.

• The nitrates synthesised by bacteria in the soil are taken up by plants and converted into amino acids, which are the building blocks of proteins. These then go through higher trophic levels of the ecosystem. During excretion and upon the death of all organisms nitrogen is returned to the soil in the form of ammonia.

• Certain quantities of soil nitrates, being highly soluble in water, are lost to the system by being transported away by surface run-off or groundwater. In the soil as well as oceans there are special denitrifying bacteria (e.g. Pseudomonas), which convert the nitrates/nitrites to elemental nitrogen. This nitrogen escapes into the atmosphere, thus completing the cycle.

• The periodic thunderstorms convert the gaseous nitrogen in the atmosphere to ammonia and nitrates which eventually reach the earth’s surface through precipitation and then into the soil to be utilized by plants.

Additional Information

• Carbon Cycle

• The carbon cycle involves several processes, including photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, and combustion. Plants absorb carbon dioxide (CO₂) during photosynthesis, while animals release CO₂ through respiration.

• Carbon is stored in various reservoirs, including the atmosphere (as CO₂), oceans (as dissolved CO₂ and organic carbon), soil (as organic matter), and living organisms. These reservoirs play a crucial role in regulating global climate.

• Human activities, such as fossil fuel combustion and deforestation, significantly alter the carbon cycle by increasing atmospheric CO₂ levels, contributing to global warming and climate change.​

• Water Cycle-

• The hydrologic cycle is the continuous circulation of water in the Earth-atmosphere system which is driven by solar energy. Water on our planet is stored in major reservoirs like atmosphere, oceans, lakes, rivers, soils, glaciers, snowfields, and groundwater. Water moves from one reservoir to another by the processes of evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, deposition, runoff, infiltration, and groundwater flow.

• Water as an important ecological factor determines the structure and function of the ecosystem. Cycling of all other nutrients is also dependent upon water as it provides their transportation during the various steps. It acts as a solvent medium for their uptake of nutrients by organisms.

• Sulphur Cycle-

• The sulphur reservoir is in the soil and sediments where it is locked in organic (coal, oil and peat) and inorganic deposits (pyrite rock and sulphur rock) in the form of sulphates, sulphides and organic sulphur.

• It is released by weathering of rocks, erosional runoff and decomposition of organic matter and is carried to terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems in a salt solution.

• The sulphur cycle is mostly sedimentary except two of its compounds hydrogen sulphide (H2S) and sulphur dioxide (SO2) add a gaseous component to its normal sedimentary cycle.

• Sulphur enters the atmosphere from several sources like volcanic eruptions, combustion of fossil fuels, from the surface of the ocean and from gases released by decomposition. Atmospheric hydrogen sulphide also gets oxidised into sulphur dioxide.

• Atmospheric sulphur dioxide is carried back to the earth after being dissolved in rainwater as weak sulphuric acid.

q: The growth form of a plant, comprising its size, shape and orientation is known as:
solution:
The correct answer is habit.

Key Points

• The term "habit" in botany refers to the general growth form of a plant, including its size, shape, and orientation.

• It describes whether the plant is a tree, shrub, herb, or vine.

• Habit is an important characteristic used to identify and classify plants.

• Understanding the habit of a plant helps in determining its ecological role and adaptability to specific environments.

Additional Information

• Environment:

• The environment is the surrounding conditions in which an organism lives, including air, water, land, and other living beings.

• It influences the growth, development, and survival of organisms but is not specific to the growth form of a plant.

• Habitat:

• The habitat is the natural environment in which a particular species lives.

• It includes all the living and non-living factors that affect the species.

• It is more about the location and environment where a species is found rather than its growth form.

• Growth Pattern:

• Growth pattern refers to the developmental process of an organism, including stages of growth and changes in form over time.

q: Name a common electrolyte disorder that occurs when the amount of sodium in your blood becomes abnormally low.
solution:
The correct answer is Hyponatremia.

Key Points

• Hyponatremia is a condition where the sodium level in the blood is lower than normal.

• Sodium is an essential electrolyte that helps regulate water balance in and around cells.

• Common causes of hyponatremia include excessive fluid intake, certain medications, and conditions like heart failure or kidney disease.

• Symptoms of hyponatremia can range from mild (nausea, headache) to severe (confusion, seizures, coma).

Additional Information

• Hyperkalemia

• Hyperkalemia is a condition characterized by an abnormally high level of potassium in the blood.

• Potassium is crucial for normal cell function, especially in the heart, muscles, and nerves.

• Causes include kidney dysfunction, excessive potassium intake, and certain medications.

• Symptoms can include muscle fatigue, weakness, paralysis, and abnormal heart rhythms.

• Hypokalemia

• Hypokalemia is a condition where there is a lower than normal level of potassium in the blood.

• It can result from conditions like chronic kidney disease, excessive loss of potassium through urine, or inadequate potassium intake.

• Symptoms may include muscle cramps, weakness, fatigue, and cardiac arrhythmias.

• Treatment typically involves potassium supplements and addressing the underlying cause.

• Hypernatremia

• Hypernatremia is a condition where the sodium level in the blood is higher than normal.

• It often occurs due to dehydration, water loss, or excessive sodium intake.

• Symptoms can include thirst, confusion, muscle twitching, and, in severe cases, seizures or coma.

• Treatment focuses on slowly rehydrating the patient and addressing the cause of the sodium imbalance.

q: What kind of phyllotaxy was examined in the Guava plant?
solution:
The correct answer is Opposite.

Key Points

• In an opposite phyllotaxy, two leaves arise at the same level from opposite sides of the stem.

• Each pair of leaves is typically perpendicular to the next pair above or below, providing a crisscross pattern.

• Opposite phyllotaxy ensures maximum light exposure for each leaf, which is beneficial for photosynthesis.

• This type of leaf arrangement is common in plants such as guava (Psidium guajava), calotropis, and jamun.

Additional Information

• Phyllotaxy

• Phyllotaxy refers to the arrangement of leaves on a plant stem.

• The primary types of phyllotaxy are alternate, opposite, and whorled.

• This arrangement plays a significant role in maximizing light capture and minimizing shading of lower leaves.

• Alternate Phyllotaxy

• In alternate phyllotaxy, each leaf arises at a different level on the stem, and the leaves are not directly opposite each other.

• Examples include sunflower and mustard.

• Whorled Phyllotaxy

• In whorled phyllotaxy, three or more leaves grow at the same level around the stem.

• This arrangement is less common and can be seen in plants like Nerium (oleander).

q: Which of the following plants is used to cure cold and cough?

Key Points

• Tulsi (Ocimum sanctum), also known as Holy Basil, is a revered medicinal plant in India.

• It is traditionally used in Ayurvedic medicine to treat cold, cough, and other respiratory ailments.

Additional Information

• Babool (Acacia nilotica)

• Babool tree has various medicinal uses, including in dental care, skin care, and as a remedy for diarrhea and dysentery.

• Its bark and leaves are commonly used in traditional medicine.

• Jamun (Syzygium cumini)

• Jamun fruit and seeds are used in Ayurvedic medicine to manage diabetes.

• It is also beneficial for digestive health and in treating ulcers.

q: Which of the following is NOT a component of a flower?
solution:
The correct answer is Spines.

Key Points

• Spines are not a component of a flower; they are modified leaves, stems, or stipules that are typically hard, pointed, and meant for protection.

• Flowers are reproductive structures in angiosperms (flowering plants) and typically consist of four main parts: androecium, corolla, calyx, and gynoecium.

• The primary role of spines is to protect the plant from herbivores and reduce water loss, especially in arid environments.

• Unlike the other options listed (androecium, corolla, and calyx), spines do not play a role in the reproductive process of the flower.

Additional Information

• Androecium

• The androecium is the collective term for the stamens in a flower. Each stamen typically consists of a filament and an anther, where pollen is produced.

• It is the male reproductive part of the flower.

• Corolla

• The corolla is the collective term for the petals of a flower.

• Petals are often brightly colored to attract pollinators.

• Calyx

• The calyx is the collective term for the sepals of a flower.

• Sepals are typically green and provide protection to the flower bud before it opens.

• Gynoecium

• The gynoecium is the collective term for the female reproductive parts of a flower, consisting of one or more carpels.

• Each carpel typically includes an ovary, style, and stigma.

q: Which of the following options indicates the size of PPLO (Pleuro Pneumonia Like Organisms)?
solution:
The correct answer is About 0.1 µm.

Key Points

• PPLOs (Pleuro Pneumonia Like Organisms) are the smallest free-living organisms known.

• They are characterized by their extremely small size, about 0.1 µm in diameter.

• PPLOs lack a cell wall, which contributes to their small size and flexible shape.

• These organisms are responsible for causing respiratory diseases, particularly in livestock.

Additional Information

• PPLO (Pleuro Pneumonia Like Organisms):

• PPLOs are a group of bacteria that belong to the class Mollicutes.

• These organisms are known for their lack of a rigid cell wall, making them resistant to antibiotics that target cell wall synthesis.

• They are often referred to as mycoplasmas, with Mycoplasma pneumoniae being a well-known species causing atypical pneumonia in humans.

• PPLOs thrive in osmotically balanced environments due to their lack of a cell wall, which makes them susceptible to osmotic lysis in hypotonic conditions.

• Importance in Research:

• The small size and simple genetic structure of PPLOs make them important models for studying the minimal requirements for cellular life.

• Research on PPLOs has provided insights into the evolution of bacteria and the mechanisms of pathogenesis in respiratory infections.

• Clinical Relevance:

• PPLOs are significant pathogens in veterinary medicine, causing respiratory diseases such as contagious bovine pleuropneumonia.

• In humans, mycoplasmas can lead to a range of respiratory and urogenital infections, requiring specific diagnostic and treatment approaches.

• Due to their lack of a cell wall, infections caused by PPLOs are treated with antibiotics that inhibit protein synthesis, such as tetracyclines or macrolides.

q: In the year 1925, who extracted lipids from an erythrocyte sample and found that lipid monolayers are good for measuring molecular surface area versus lateral pressure?
solution:
The correct answer is Gorter and Grendel.

Key Points

• In 1925, Dutch scientists Evert Gorter and François Grendel conducted a groundbreaking experiment involving erythrocyte (red blood cell) lipid extraction.

• They found that the lipids extracted from erythrocytes could form a monolayer, which was pivotal in understanding the molecular surface area versus lateral pressure.

• Their work was fundamental in the development of the fluid mosaic model of cell membranes.

• Gorter and Grendel's experiment was one of the first to suggest that cell membranes are composed of a lipid bilayer.

Additional Information

• Lipid Monolayers and Bilayers:

• A lipid monolayer is a single layer of lipid molecules arranged on the surface of the water, with their hydrophobic tails in the air and hydrophilic heads in the water.

• A lipid bilayer is a double layer of lipids that form the fundamental structure of cell membranes, with hydrophobic tails facing inward and hydrophilic heads facing outward.

• These structures are crucial for maintaining the integrity and functionality of cell membranes.

• Erythrocytes (Red Blood Cells):

• Erythrocytes are the most common type of blood cell and are responsible for transporting oxygen from the lungs to the body's tissues and carbon dioxide from the tissues back to the lungs.

• Their membrane composition and properties are essential for their deformability and functionality.

• Surface Area vs. Lateral Pressure:

• This concept involves measuring the surface area occupied by lipid molecules as a function of the lateral pressure applied to the monolayer.

• It is used to study the physical properties of lipid layers and understand cell membrane mechanics.

• Fluid Mosaic Model:

• Proposed by Singer and Nicolson in 1972, this model describes the cell membrane as a fluid combination of lipids and proteins.

• The lipids provide a flexible matrix, while proteins float in or on this lipid bilayer, contributing to various cellular functions.

q: Which set of diseases are caused by bacteria?
solution:
The correct answer is Typhoid, Cholera, Tuberculosis.

Key Points

• Typhoid fever is caused by the bacterium Salmonella typhi and is typically spread through contaminated food and water.

• Cholera is caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae and is also usually spread through contaminated water and food, leading to severe diarrhea and dehydration.

• Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis and primarily affects the lungs, but can also affect other parts of the body.

• These diseases are treatable with antibiotics, which target and kill the bacterial pathogens responsible for the infections.

Additional Information

• Influenza

• Influenza, also known as the flu, is caused by influenza viruses, not bacteria.

• It is a contagious respiratory illness with symptoms like fever, cough, and body aches.

• Vaccines are available to help prevent influenza.

• Dengue

• Dengue is caused by the dengue virus, which is transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes.

• It leads to symptoms such as high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, joint and muscle pain, and rash.

• There is no specific treatment for dengue, but supportive care can help manage symptoms.

• Malaria

• Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites, which are transmitted through the bites of infected Anopheles mosquitoes.

• Symptoms include fever, chills, and flu-like illness; if not treated, it can lead to severe complications and death.

• Antimalarial drugs are used to treat and prevent malaria.

• Common Cold

• The common cold is caused by a variety of viruses, most commonly rhinoviruses.

• It is characterized by symptoms such as sneezing, runny nose, and sore throat.

• There is no cure for the common cold, but symptoms can be managed with over-the-counter medications.

q: Which is a serious contagious bacterial infection that usually affects the mucous membranes of the nose and throat?
solution:
The correct answer is Diphtheria.

*Key Points

• Diphtheria is a serious bacterial infection that usually affects the mucous membranes of the nose and throat.

• The disease is caused by the bacterium Corynebacterium diphtheriae*.

• Diphtheria spreads through respiratory droplets from coughing or sneezing.

• Symptoms include a thick, gray membrane covering the throat and tonsils, sore throat, swollen glands, and difficulty breathing.

*Additional Information

• Meningococcal Disease

• Meningococcal disease is caused by the bacterium Neisseria meningitidis*.

• It can lead to serious infections such as meningitis (inflammation of the membranes around the brain and spinal cord) and septicemia (blood poisoning).

• The disease spreads through respiratory droplets and close contact with an infected person.

• Symptoms include sudden fever, headache, and a stiff neck, often accompanied by nausea, vomiting, sensitivity to light, and altered mental status.

• Shigellosis

• Shigellosis is an infectious disease caused by a group of bacteria called *Shigella*.

• It is characterized by diarrhea (often bloody), fever, and stomach cramps.

• The infection spreads through contaminated food, water, or contact with an infected person.

• Good hygiene practices, especially handwashing, are critical for preventing the spread of Shigellosis.

• Chlamydia

• Chlamydia is a common sexually transmitted infection (STI) caused by the bacterium *Chlamydia trachomatis*.

• It can infect both men and women, causing damage to the reproductive system.

• Symptoms may include abnormal genital discharge and a burning sensation during urination.

• If left untreated, Chlamydia can lead to serious reproductive and other health problems with both short-term and long-term consequences.

q: Which of the following pairs is INCORRECTLY matched?
solution:
The correct answer is Starch: Egg yolk.

Key Points

• Starch is a carbohydrate consisting of a large number of glucose units joined by glycosidic bonds.

• It is produced by most green plants as an energy store.

• Egg yolk does not contain starch; it is rich in proteins and fats.

• Common sources of starch include potatoes, rice, wheat, and corn.

Additional Information

• Lactose

• Lactose is a disaccharide sugar derived from galactose and glucose that is found in milk.

• It makes up around 2-8% of milk (by weight).

• Lactose is important for the proper digestion of milk in mammals.

• Fructose

• Fructose is a simple sugar found in many plants, where it is often bonded to glucose to form the disaccharide sucrose.

• It is one of the three dietary monosaccharides, along with glucose and galactose, that are absorbed directly into the bloodstream during digestion.

• Fructose is commonly found in fruits such as grapes, apples, and honey.

• Maltose

• Maltose, also known as malt sugar, is a disaccharide formed from two units of glucose joined with an α(1→4) bond.

• It is found in germinating grains like wheat, cornmeal, and barley.

• Maltose is used in the brewing of beer and is a component of malt.

• Hydra is a genus of small, fresh-water organisms of the phylum Cnidaria and class Hydrozoa.

q: Which marine carotenoid is abundant in brown seaweed, macroalgae and diatoms?
solution:
The correct answer is Fucoxanthin.

Key Points

• Fucoxanthin is a marine carotenoid found in brown algae such as wakame and hijiki.

• It is responsible for giving brown seaweed its characteristic color.

• Fucoxanthin has been studied for its potential health benefits, including its effects on metabolism and weight management.

• It also possesses antioxidant properties, which help in protecting cells from damage.

Additional Information

• Carotenoids:

• Carotenoids are pigments found in plants, algae, and photosynthetic bacteria. They play a critical role in plant health by absorbing light energy for use in photosynthesis.

• They are divided into two classes: xanthophylls (which contain oxygen) and carotenes (which are purely hydrocarbons and contain no oxygen).

• Carotenoids are important for human health as they have antioxidant properties and can be converted into vitamin A in the body.

• Astaxanthin:

• Astaxanthin is another marine carotenoid, primarily found in microalgae, shrimp, and salmon. It is known for its strong antioxidant properties.

• It is often used as a dietary supplement for its potential health benefits, including eye and skin health, and anti-inflammatory effects.

• Neoxanthin:

• Neoxanthin is a type of xanthophyll found in green leafy vegetables and plays a role in the light-harvesting complex of photosynthesis.

• It has been studied for its potential anti-cancer properties.

• β-cryptoxanthin:

• β-cryptoxanthin is a carotenoid found in fruits such as oranges, papayas, and tangerines.

• It is a provitamin A carotenoid, meaning it can be converted into vitamin A in the body.

• It has been associated with various health benefits, including bone health and reducing the risk of certain chronic diseases.

q: Filtration of waste products in humans happens in the kidneys. There is a large number of filtration units present inside the kidneys to help them in doing this job. These filtration units are called:
solution:
The correct answer is nephrons.

Key Points

• Nephrons are the basic structural and functional units of the kidney.

• Each kidney contains around 1 to 1.5 million nephrons.

• Nephrons are responsible for the removal of waste products, excess substances, and toxins from the blood.

• They play a crucial role in the regulation of water, electrolytes, and maintaining the body's acid-base balance.

Additional Information

• Bowman's Capsule

• The Bowman's capsule is a cup-like sac at the beginning of the nephron in the kidney.

• It encases the glomerulus and is involved in the first step of the filtration of blood to form urine.

• It captures the filtrate produced from the blood and passes it into the renal tubule.

• Capillaries

• Capillaries are the smallest blood vessels in the body.

• They facilitate the exchange of oxygen, carbon dioxide, nutrients, and waste products between blood and tissues.

• In the kidneys, capillaries are part of the glomerulus and play a critical role in the filtration process.

• Alveoli

• Alveoli are small air sacs in the lungs where gas exchange takes place.

• Oxygen from the inhaled air passes through the walls of the alveoli and into the blood in the capillaries, while carbon dioxide from the blood passes into the alveoli to be exhaled.

• They are crucial for efficient respiratory function but are not related to kidney function.

q: Identify a spiral-shaped bacteria.
solution:
The correct answer is Spirillum.

Key Points

• Spirillum is a genus of Gram-negative bacteria characterized by their spiral shape.

• They are typically found in stagnant freshwater environments and are known for their unique helical structure.

• Spirillum bacteria are motile, meaning they can move, using flagella located at both ends of the cell.

• These bacteria are often used in microbiological studies to understand bacterial motility and structure.

Additional Information

• Bacillus

• Bacillus is a genus of rod-shaped, Gram-positive bacteria.

• These bacteria are commonly found in soil and water and are known for their ability to form endospores.

• Examples include Bacillus anthracis, which causes anthrax, and Bacillus subtilis, a model organism for laboratory studies.

• Coccus

• Coccus refers to any bacterium that has a spherical, ovoid, or generally round shape.

• They can exist as single cells or in clusters, chains, and other formations.

• Examples include Staphylococcus (clusters) and Streptococcus (chains).

• Vibrio

• Vibrio is a genus of Gram-negative bacteria, possessing a curved-rod (comma) shape.

• They are typically aquatic and can cause diseases such as cholera (caused by Vibrio cholerae).

• Vibrio bacteria are facultative anaerobes, meaning they can survive with or without oxygen.

q: Which of the following is NOT related to reticulate venation?
solution:
The correct answer is Maize.

Key Points

• Maize exhibits parallel venation, which is typical of monocotyledonous plants.

• In parallel venation, veins run parallel to each other, which is different from reticulate venation where veins form a network.

• Examples of plants with parallel venation include grasses, lilies, and maize.

• Reticulate venation is commonly found in dicotyledonous plants like China rose and Tulsi.

Additional Information

• Venation

• Venation refers to the arrangement of veins in the leaf blade.

• It is important for the identification of plant species and helps in the distribution of nutrients and water throughout the leaf.

• Reticulate Venation

• Reticulate venation is characterized by a net-like pattern of veins.

• It is commonly found in dicots such as China rose, Tulsi, and Coriander.

• In this type of venation, the main vein (midrib) branches into secondary veins which further branch into tertiary veins forming a network.

• Parallel Venation

• Parallel venation is characterized by veins running parallel to each other.

• It is typical of monocots such as Maize, wheat, and other grasses.

• In this type of venation, veins do not form a network but run parallel from the base to the tip of the leaf.

• Examples of Plants

• China Rose (Hibiscus rosa-sinensis) - Exhibits reticulate venation.

• Tulsi (Ocimum tenuiflorum) - Exhibits reticulate venation.

• Maize (Zea mays) - Exhibits parallel venation.

• Coriander (Coriandrum sativum) - Exhibits reticulate venation.

q: Which of the following is an example of prokaryotic cells?
solution:
The correct answer is Bacteria.

Key Points

• Bacteria are single-celled organisms that lack a nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles, making them prokaryotic.

• Bacteria are among the most ancient and diverse forms of life on Earth, thriving in various environments.

• Bacteria can be classified into various shapes such as cocci (spherical), bacilli (rod-shaped), and spirilla (spiral-shaped).

• Bacteria play crucial roles in processes like nutrient cycling, fermentation, and as part of the microbiome in various organisms.

Additional Information

• Prokaryotic Cells

• Prokaryotic cells are primitive cells that lack a well-defined nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.

• They have a simple cell structure with genetic material (DNA) present in a nucleoid region.

• Examples include Bacteria and Archaea.

• Eukaryotic Cells

• Eukaryotic cells have a well-defined nucleus and various membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, and Golgi apparatus.

• These cells are more complex and are found in organisms such as animals, plants, fungi, and protists.

• Examples include Plasmodium (a protist), Leishmania (a protist), and Yeast (a fungus).

• Plasmodium

• Plasmodium is a genus of parasitic protozoa that causes malaria in humans and other animals.

• It is a eukaryotic organism with a complex life cycle involving both an insect vector (mosquito) and a vertebrate host.

• Leishmania

• Leishmania is a genus of protozoan parasites, transmitted by the bite of infected sandflies.

• It causes diseases known as leishmaniasis in humans.

• Yeast

• Yeast is a type of fungus that is used in baking, brewing, and scientific research.

• It is a eukaryotic microorganism with a well-defined nucleus and other organelles.

q: Which of the following illustrations is related to chloroplasts?
solution:
The correct answer is 2) c.

Key Points

• Chloroplasts are organelles found in plant cells and eukaryotic algae that conduct photosynthesis.

• Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, a green pigment that captures light energy.

• They are surrounded by a double membrane and contain their own DNA, similar to mitochondria.

• The main function of chloroplasts is to convert solar energy into chemical energy in the form of glucose through photosynthesis.

Additional Information

• Photosynthesis

• It is the process by which green plants and some other organisms use sunlight to synthesize foods with the help of chlorophyll.

• Photosynthesis involves the conversion of carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.

• The general equation for photosynthesis is: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light energy = C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.

• Chlorophyll

• Chlorophyll is the molecule that absorbs sunlight and uses its energy to synthesize carbohydrates from CO₂ and water.

• It is what gives plants their green color.

• Thylakoids

• Thylakoids are membrane-bound compartments inside chloroplasts and cyanobacteria.

• They are the site of the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis.

• Thylakoids are arranged in stacks known as grana.

• Stroma

• Stroma is the fluid-filled space that surrounds the grana inside the chloroplast.

• It is the site of the light-independent reactions (Calvin cycle) of photosynthesis.

q: Which is the most important protein component in milk, both quantitatively and nutritionally, that accounts for about 80% of the total protein in bovine milk?
solution:
The correct answer is Casein.

Key Points

• Casein is the most abundant protein in milk, making up about 80% of the total protein content in bovine milk.

• It is nutritionally valuable due to its high quality and rich composition of essential amino acids.

• Casein proteins are slow-digesting, providing a sustained release of amino acids into the bloodstream.

• It plays an important role in providing the necessary nutrients for the growth and development of young mammals.

Additional Information

• Actin

• Actin is a protein that forms microfilaments and is involved in various types of cell motility and structure.

• It is not a major component of milk but is essential in muscle contraction and cellular movements.

• Albumin

• Albumin is a type of protein found in blood plasma, egg white, and milk.

• While it is present in milk, it does not constitute the majority of milk proteins.

• It is important for maintaining the osmotic pressure necessary for proper distribution of body fluids between body tissues and the bloodstream.

• Pepsin

• Pepsin is a digestive enzyme that breaks down proteins into peptides.

• It is produced in the stomach and is not a component of milk.

• It functions in the digestive system to help in the digestion of proteins from food.

• Casein

• Casein is a family of related phosphoproteins that are commonly found in mammalian milk.

• It forms a gel or clot in the stomach, which makes it very efficient in nutrient supply.

• Casein is used in cheese-making and as a food additive for its binding properties.

• Its ability to provide a slow and sustained release of amino acids makes it highly beneficial for muscle repair and growth.

q: What is the other name of tetanus caused by toxin producing bacteria called clostridium tetani?
solution:
The correct answer is Lockjaw.

Key Points

• Lockjaw is a common name for tetanus, a serious bacterial infection.

• Tetanus is caused by the bacterium Clostridium tetani, which produces a toxin affecting the nervous system.

• The condition is characterized by muscle stiffness and spasms, particularly in the jaw muscles, hence the name "lockjaw".

• Without treatment, tetanus can be fatal, but it is preventable through vaccination.

Additional Information

• Clostridium tetani:

• It is a spore-forming bacterium found in soil, dust, and animal feces.

• The spores can enter the body through wounds, especially deep puncture wounds, and produce a toxin called tetanospasmin.

• Tetanospasmin interferes with the nervous system, leading to severe muscle spasms.

• Tetanus Symptoms:

• Symptoms typically appear 3 to 21 days after infection.

• Common symptoms include muscle stiffness, difficulty swallowing, and jaw cramping (lockjaw).

• Severe cases can lead to muscle spasms in the back, neck, and other parts of the body.

• Tetanus Treatment:

• Treatment usually involves wound care, medications to control muscle spasms, and antibiotics to fight the infection.

• In severe cases, patients may require hospitalization and supportive care, including mechanical ventilation.

• Tetanus Prevention:

• The best way to prevent tetanus is through vaccination.

• The DTaP (diphtheria, tetanus, and acellular pertussis) vaccine is routinely given to children, and booster shots (Td or Tdap) are recommended for adults every 10 years.

• Proper wound care and hygiene can also help prevent tetanus infection.

q: Who published Systema Naturae in 1735 classifying the three kingdoms of nature and outlining the sexual system for the classification of plants?
solution:
The correct answer is Carolus Linnaeus.

Key Points

• Carolus Linnaeus, also known as Carl Linnaeus or Carl von Linné, was a Swedish botanist, zoologist, and physician.

• He published the landmark book "Systema Naturae" in 1735, which laid the foundations for the modern biological naming scheme of binomial nomenclature.

• Linnaeus classified nature into three kingdoms: animal, vegetable, and mineral, and introduced the sexual system for the classification of plants.

• His work in "Systema Naturae" is considered one of the most significant contributions to the field of taxonomy and systematics.

Additional Information

• Systema Naturae

• Systema Naturae is one of the major works of Carl Linnaeus and was first published in 1735.

• It introduced a hierarchical classification system, which is the basis for the modern system of taxonomy.

• The book included a classification of all known plants, animals, and minerals, and established the use of binomial nomenclature, where each species is given a two-part Latin name (genus and species).

• The sexual system of plant classification was based on the number and arrangement of reproductive organs (stamens and pistils).

• Binomial Nomenclature

• Binomial nomenclature is a formal system of naming species of living things by giving each a name composed of two parts, both of which use Latin grammatical forms.

• The first part of the name identifies the genus to which the species belongs, and the second part identifies the species within the genus.

• This system was developed by Carolus Linnaeus and is used universally in the scientific community.

• Taxonomy

• Taxonomy is the science of defining and naming groups of biological organisms based on shared characteristics.

• Organisms are grouped into taxa, which are then grouped into larger taxa, creating a hierarchical structure.

• Linnaeus' classification system included ranks such as kingdom, class, order, family, genus, and species, which are still used today.

• Sexual System

• The sexual system was a method of classifying plants based on the number and arrangement of their reproductive organs.

• This system was part of Linnaeus' work in "Systema Naturae" and was revolutionary at the time, providing a clear and structured way to classify plants.

q: By which of the following methods do red algae reproduce?

• Fragmentation in red algae can occur naturally due to water currents, or it can be induced by external factors such as being grazed by herbivores.

• Grafting is a horticultural technique where tissues from one plant are inserted into those of another so that the two sets of vascular tissues may join together.

• It is commonly used in agriculture and horticulture to propagate clones of desired plants.

• Cutting

• Cutting is a method of plant propagation where a piece of the plant, typically a stem or leaf, is cut and placed in a suitable environment to grow into a new plant.

• It is widely used for the propagation of houseplants and garden plants.

• Micropropagation

• Micropropagation is a method used to multiply plants under sterile conditions, often from very small plant parts, such as cells or tissues.

• It is used for the rapid multiplication of plants and the production of disease-free plants.

• Fragmentation

• As mentioned, fragmentation is a form of asexual reproduction where an organism is split into fragments, each capable of growing independently into a new organism.

• It is a common method of reproduction in many algae, including red algae, as well as in some plants and fungi.

q: Which types of gametes are found in Spirogyra?
solution:
The correct answer is Isogamous and non-flagellated.

Key Points

• Spirogyra is a genus of filamentous green algae that is commonly found in fresh water.

• The gametes in Spirogyra are isogamous, meaning they are morphologically similar or identical.

• Isogamous gametes in Spirogyra are non-flagellated, meaning they do not have flagella and thus do not have the ability to move independently.

• During reproduction, Spirogyra undergoes a process called conjugation, where gametes from different filaments join together to form a zygote.

Additional Information

• Isogamy:

• Isogamy refers to a type of sexual reproduction involving gametes of similar morphology (shape and size), differing only in their allelic composition.

• In isogamous species, the gametes are often referred to as "+" and "-" types rather than male and female.

• Flagella:

• Flagella are long, whip-like appendages that protrude from the cell body and enable many protozoa, bacteria, and spermatozoa to swim.

• Non-flagellated gametes lack these appendages and thus rely on other means for movement, such as water currents.

• Conjugation in Spirogyra:

• Conjugation in Spirogyra is a form of sexual reproduction where two filaments align side by side and form conjugation tubes.

• Protoplasts from one filament move through these tubes and fuse with the protoplasts of the other filament to form zygospores.

• Zygospores are thick-walled and can survive harsh conditions. Upon germination, they undergo meiosis to produce new haploid filaments.

• Spirogyra:

• Spirogyra is known for its spiral arrangement of chloroplasts, which is unique and easily identifiable.

• It is commonly referred to as "pond scum" and can form dense mats on the surface of freshwater bodies.

• Spirogyra plays an important role in the ecosystem by producing oxygen through photosynthesis and serving as food for aquatic organisms.

q: Which of the following researchers observed densely stained reticular structures surrounding the nucleus (Hint: Figure)?
solution:
The correct answer is Camillo Golgi.

Key Points

• Camillo Golgi was an Italian physician, pathologist, and scientist.

• He is renowned for discovering the Golgi apparatus, a complex of vesicles and folded membranes within the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells.

• The Golgi apparatus plays a critical role in sorting and packaging proteins and lipids for secretion or delivery to other organelles.

• Golgi's discovery was a pivotal moment in cell biology, and he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1906 for his contributions.

Additional Information

• Golgi Apparatus

• The Golgi apparatus, also known as the Golgi complex, is an organelle found in most eukaryotic cells.

• It is involved in the modification, sorting, and packaging of proteins and lipids for secretion or use within the cell.

• The Golgi apparatus is composed of a series of flattened, stacked pouches called cisternae.

• The cis face of the Golgi apparatus is the receiving side, while the trans face is the shipping side.

• Camillo Golgi's Contributions

• Camillo Golgi developed a staining technique called the "black reaction" or "Golgi stain," which allowed him to visualize the Golgi apparatus and other cellular structures.

• This staining method involves using silver nitrate to selectively stain the nervous system tissue, enabling the detailed study of neurons and their connections.

• Golgi's work laid the foundation for our understanding of the organization and function of the nervous system.

• His discoveries have had a lasting impact on the field of cell biology and neuroscience.

• Other Notable Researchers

• William Harvey: An English physician who made significant contributions to the understanding of the circulatory system, particularly the function of the heart and blood vessels.

• Francis Crick: A British molecular biologist, biophysicist, and neuroscientist who co-discovered the structure of DNA with James Watson.

• Louis Pasteur: A French biologist, microbiologist, and chemist renowned for his discoveries of the principles of vaccination, microbial fermentation, and pasteurization.

q: In the context of cell division, which chromosomal behaviour takes place at the leptotene stage?
solution:
The correct answer is Chromosomes begin to condense.

Key Points

• During the leptotene stage, chromosomes start to condense and become visible under a microscope.

• This stage is the initial phase of prophase I in meiosis, where chromosomes appear as long, thread-like structures.

• The condensation of chromosomes helps in their subsequent alignment and pairing during meiosis.

• Chromosomal condensation is crucial for the accurate segregation of chromosomes into daughter cells.

Additional Information

• Leptotene Stage

• The leptotene stage is the first stage of prophase I in meiosis.

• During this stage, chromosomes start to condense and become visible as thin threads.

• It is followed by the zygotene stage, where homologous chromosomes begin to pair and synapse.

• Meiosis

• Meiosis is a type of cell division that reduces the chromosome number by half, resulting in four genetically distinct daughter cells.

• It consists of two consecutive divisions: meiosis I and meiosis II.

• Meiosis is essential for sexual reproduction and contributes to genetic diversity.

• Chromosomal Synapsis

• Synapsis is the pairing of homologous chromosomes during prophase I of meiosis.

• It occurs during the zygotene stage, following the leptotene stage.

• Synapsis is crucial for the exchange of genetic material between homologous chromosomes through crossing over.
